title: Nepal moves to declare 213 Indians missing since August flash flood presumed dead
dek: Families have until 2 December to raise objections to the list, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu said. The 26 August flood, set off by an ice-rock collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border, killed at least 1,453 people.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Nepal has begun the legal process of presuming and declaring dead 213 Indian nationals who have been missing since the flash flood that tore through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli valleys on 26 August, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu said on Wednesday.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has published the list of the 213 names on its website and invited objections, additions and corrections, the embassy said in a press release. Families with concerns about the list have until 2 December to contact the embassy, which has set up a dedicated email address and phone helpline. Once Nepal finalises the list and formally issues the declarations of death, the embassy will start obtaining death certificates for the families from local authorities in Nepal. It said it might ask families for further details and documents.

## Why the declarations matter

For three months, the families of the missing have been unable to obtain death certificates, because Nepal issues them only when a death is confirmed at a hospital or a body is identified. Without a certificate, relatives cannot settle insurance claims or property, or apply for compensation. In September the embassy asked families to help identify recovered bodies through photographs on the Nepal Police website and by sending DNA profiles.

The number of Indians unaccounted for has fallen as people were traced. In the days after the flood, the Indian government said 320 of its citizens could not be contacted, according to reports at the time.

## The disaster

The flood, Nepal's deadliest in decades, killed at least 1,453 people and left more than 5,000 missing, according to the NDRRMA. These figures include Nepalis and foreigners. It was set off when a mass of ice and rock fell from a slope near the Nepal-Tibet border and briefly dammed a stream before bursting, according to reports. The water swept through Rasuwa district, including the town of Syabrubesi, and down the Trishuli river through Nuwakot and Dhading. Authorities in China's Tibet Autonomous Region reported deaths and missing people on their side too.

Many of the Indians who went missing were pilgrims. The Rasuwagadhi-Gyirong crossing is the main road route from Nepal to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar in Tibet, and hundreds of pilgrims bound for Kailash lost contact after a checkpoint on the route was destroyed, according to reports. The flood also damaged at least six hydropower and transmission facilities, cutting about 431 MW from Nepal's grid, and Nepal's finance minister put reconstruction costs at $4-5 billion, according to reports.

## The cross-border warning gap

The disaster exposed the lack of a working real-time system for sharing hazard data across the Himalayas. Nepal and China agreed after a smaller glacial flood in July 2025 to share cross-border data, but had not signed a formal agreement by the time of the August flood, according to reports from Kathmandu. Nepal's hydrology department learned of the flood about 16 minutes after it crossed the border, those reports said. China's embassy in Nepal rejected claims that a dam on the Chinese side had failed, describing the event as a geological collapse, and Chinese officials have denied withholding warnings.

The same question matters to India downstream. India's agreements with China to receive flood-season river data on the Sutlej and the Brahmaputra expired in 2020 and 2023 and have not been renewed, and India's Jal Shakti ministry has said China has shared no hydrological data since 2022. Nepal's rivers, meanwhile, feed the Ganga basin that runs through Bihar and West Bengal.

## What happens next

After the 2 December deadline, Nepal will finalise the list and issue the formal declarations. The step comes days after Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah made his first bilateral visit to India, where the two sides discussed energy, connectivity and trade, according to reports.
